title: Tesla FSD & Optimus Product Review
summary: Product review across autonomy and Optimus. Decisions: hold the robotaxi fleet at current size in Austin until the unprotected-left intervention rate improves 3x, expand to Phoenix only after that gate, freeze the Optimus V3 hand design for both the Mars payload and the pilot production line, and shift 20 percent of FSD training compute to Optimus manipulation for the quarter. Taneja flagged Optimus line capex phasing; agreed to gate the second line on first-line yield.
decisions: Hold Austin robotaxi fleet size flat until unprotected-left intervention rate improves 3x
Phoenix expansion is gated on the Austin intervention metric, not the calendar
Freeze Optimus V3 hand design on August 15 for both the Mars payload and the pilot line
Reallocate 20 percent of FSD training compute to Optimus manipulation training this quarter
Second Optimus production line capex is gated on first-line yield reaching 85 percent

action_items.task: Ship the unprotected-left improvements in FSD v14.3 and report the new intervention rate weekly
Deliver the frozen Optimus V3 hand spec with the Mars environmental deltas documented
Rework the Optimus capex plan with the second line gated on yield, for the September board deck
Sign the shared Optimus freeze spec with SpaceX so the Mars payload and factory build match

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Alright, two hours flew in from Starbase for this so let's make it count. FSD first, then Optimus, then Vaibhav tells us what we can't afford. Ashok, robotaxi numbers. Real ones, not the chart for the shareholders.

transcript.speaker: Ashok Elluswamy
transcript.text: Real ones. Austin fleet is at four hundred and twelve cars, fully driverless, about nine thousand paid rides a day. Critical disengagement rate is one per twenty-nine thousand miles, which is up 40 percent from May. The problem child is unprotected left turns at high-speed intersections — that's 31 percent of all interventions, and it hasn't moved in eight weeks.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Why hasn't it moved? We threw v14.2 at it.

transcript.speaker: Ashok Elluswamy
transcript.text: v14.2 improved the perception side — we track cross-traffic velocity better. What's left is a behavior problem: the model is too conservative in gaps humans would take, so it waits, then riders report it as stuck, and remote operators nudge it. When we tune assertiveness up in sim, we start seeing gap acceptance we're not comfortable shipping. The fix we believe in is training on the specific intersection geometries — we've mined 2.3 million unprotected-left clips from the fleet and we're building a targeted curriculum. That's the core of v14.3.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Okay. Here's my position and I know marketing will hate it: we do not add cars in Austin and we do not touch Phoenix until unprotected lefts improve 3x. The robotaxi business lives or dies on the safety record, one bad-judgment left turn on video undoes a year of progress. Growth is gated on the metric, not the calendar.

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.text: For the record I support that, but it has an earnings-call consequence — we guided to three cities by Q4. If Phoenix is metric-gated I need to reframe the guidance language in October. Better to reframe than to miss, so I'll draft it, but you own saying it on the call, Elon, not me.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: I'll say it. 'Gated on safety metrics' is a sentence I'm happy to defend. Ashok, when does v14.3 ship and what's the honest probability it gets the 3x?

transcript.speaker: Ashok Elluswamy
transcript.text: Ships to the internal fleet August 27th. Honest probability of a full 3x from one release, maybe 40 percent. Getting 2x is likely; the rest may need the intersection-priors work which lands in 14.4. So realistically Phoenix is a November decision.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Fine, November, and I want the intervention rate in my inbox every Monday. Okay, Optimus. Franz, we have a very hard deadline on this one — August 15 the Mars payload config freezes, and I'd rather the flight units and the production line build the same robot. Where's the hand?

transcript.speaker: Franz von Holzhausen
transcript.text: The V3 hand is genuinely done, and I'm saying that as the person who un-did it twice. Twenty-two degrees of freedom, tendon-driven, the new fingertip sensors give us 0.1-newton force resolution. It survived the thousand-hour durability run, it can pick up an egg and also carry forty pounds. The Mars question is different though — it's environmental. Dust ingress and thermal. Mars-rated seals and lubricants add mass and cost that the factory version doesn't need.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: So one hand design, two trim levels. Same kinematics, same control stack, different seals. Can you document the Mars deltas as a bolt-on package so the training transfers one to one?

transcript.speaker: Ashok Elluswamy
transcript.text: That's the key requirement from my side. If the kinematics and sensor response are identical, every hour of manipulation training on Earth transfers directly to the Mars units. If the seals change the friction profile, we can calibrate that out in software as long as we know it before the freeze.

transcript.speaker: Franz von Holzhausen
transcript.text: You'll have the frozen spec with the Mars delta package documented by the 15th. One ask back: after the freeze, no drive-by upgrades. Elon, you walked the line three weeks ago and we lost four days to the forearm cable routing idea. It was a good idea. It's a 2027 idea.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Guilty. That's exactly why I'm signing the freeze spec myself — same document SpaceX gets. After the 15th, the next hand revision is V4 and it goes through change control like everyone else's ideas. Painful but correct. Okay — what do the Mars robots actually do on day one? Ashok, the autonomy story on Mars, twenty-minute light delay, no teleoperation rescue.

transcript.speaker: Ashok Elluswamy
transcript.text: Three mission behaviors, in order of ambition. One: egress — walk off the ship, survive terrain, that alone is historic. Two: deploy and connect the solar arrays, which is the mission-critical one because everything downstream needs power. Three, stretch goal: inspect the other ships and photograph them. Everything runs autonomously with Earth review at each phase gate — we approve the plan, not the steps. The gap I'm worried about is manipulation robustness in dust-on-connector scenarios, which is why I want more training compute.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: How much more?

transcript.speaker: Ashok Elluswamy
transcript.text: Twenty percent of the FSD training allocation for the quarter. FSD can afford it — v14.3's curriculum is data-limited, not compute-limited, the bottleneck is clip curation. Optimus manipulation is the opposite, compute-limited: we have the teleop demonstration data, we need the sim scale-up for the dust and glove variations.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Approved — twenty percent for the quarter, and it snaps back to FSD on November 1 no matter what, because 14.4 will need it. Vaibhav, you've been quiet, which is always expensive. Go.

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.text: The Optimus pilot line. The plan of record has line one ramping to a thousand units a month by December and committing capex for line two in October. Line one is currently at about two hundred a month with a 61 percent first-pass yield — the actuator install and the hand calibration are the yield killers. Committing line two capex while line one yields 61 percent is how you burn nine figures memorializing your process problems in duplicate. I want line two gated on line one hitting 85 percent yield.

transcript.speaker: Franz von Holzhausen
transcript.text: Supporting data point: half the yield loss is the hand calibration station, and that improves automatically once the design freezes — the station's been chasing a moving spec. Freeze on the 15th and I'd expect yield in the high seventies by October without heroics.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: I hate gates on manufacturing ramps and I also just imposed one on robotaxi, so consistency wins. Fine — line two capex is gated on 85 percent yield at line one. But Vaibhav, pre-position the long-lead equipment orders with cancellation clauses so the gate costs us weeks, not quarters, when we clear it.

transcript.speaker: Vaibhav Taneja
transcript.text: That's exactly the structure I'll build — reworked capex plan with the gate and the pre-positioned long-leads, in the September board deck. One more flag: the Mars payload units. Thirty flight robots plus spares, Mars-rated, is roughly a 90 million line item with the environmental qual. I need to know which company pays — Tesla building them means related-party disclosure with SpaceX as the customer.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: SpaceX buys them at cost plus audit, same structure as the Starlink terminal arrangement, papered before the freeze date. Boring and clean. Okay, recap: robotaxi growth gated on a 3x on unprotected lefts, weekly metric to me; Phoenix is a November decision; hand freezes on the 15th, one design with a Mars delta package, and I sign it; twenty percent compute to Optimus until November 1; line two gated on 85 percent yield with long-leads pre-positioned; SpaceX buys the Mars units at cost. Anyone disagree with anything? Now is the time, not in six weeks.

transcript.speaker: Ashok Elluswamy
transcript.text: No disagreement. One request — when you talk about the Mars robots publicly, say 'attempt.' The team's confidence is high on egress, medium on solar deploy. If the world expects a robot base and gets one robot walking, we lose a news cycle we earned.

transcript.speaker: Elon Musk
transcript.text: Fair. Public framing is: first attempt, success is walking off the ship, anything more is a bonus. Which happens to be true, which is the best kind of framing. Alright — this was a good one. Franz, freeze the hand. Ashok, fix the left turns. Vaibhav, keep us honest. I'm back to Starbase.
